what_its_for: Insulin glargine-yfgn is a long-acting insulin used to help control blood sugar levels in adults and children (6 years and older) with type 1 diabetes, and in adults with type 2 diabetes. It works around the clock to keep your blood sugar from getting too high.
how_to_take: Inject this insulin under your skin (subcutaneous injection) once a day, at the same time every day. Common injection sites include your stomach area (abdomen), upper thighs, or upper arms. Rotate your injection sites each time to avoid skin problems. Never inject into a vein or muscle. Do not mix this insulin with any other insulin in the same syringe. Always use a new needle for each injection to keep it clean and reduce discomfort.
dosing: Your doctor will prescribe the dose that is right for you based on your blood sugar levels, diet, activity level, and other medicines. Do not change your dose on your own without talking to your doctor or diabetes care team first. Your dose may need to be adjusted over time.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, check your blood sugar and contact your doctor or diabetes care team for guidance on what dose to take and when. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Try to get back on your regular once-daily schedule as soon as possible.
storage: Store unopened (unused) pens or vials in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze insulin glargine-yfgn, and do not use it if it has been frozen. Once you start using a pen or vial, you can keep it at room temperature (below 86°F or 30°C) and out of direct heat and light for up to 28 days. Always keep the cap on the pen when not in use. Throw away any open pen or vial after 28 days, even if there is insulin left in it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol, as it can cause unpredictable changes in your blood sugar. Do not skip meals after taking your insulin. Avoid changing your diet, exercise routine, or other medicines without first talking to your doctor. Do not share your insulin pen, needles, or syringes with anyone else, even if the needle has been changed, as this can spread infections. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if your blood sugar is low.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency help if you have signs of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) such as shakiness, sweating, dizziness, confusion, fast heartbeat, or fainting. Also call your doctor if you have signs of high blood sugar (hyperglycemia) such as increased thirst, frequent urination, blurry vision, or fruity-smelling breath. Seek emergency care for signs of a serious allergic reaction including rash, itching, trouble breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, or throat. Contact your doctor if you notice skin thickening, pitting, or lumps at your injection sites.
when_it_works: Insulin glargine-yfgn is a long-acting insulin that starts working within 1 to 2 hours after injection and continues to work evenly for up to 24 hours. It does not have a sharp peak like some other insulins. You may notice improvements in your blood sugar levels within the first few days, but it may take a week or more to find the right dose for you.
special_populations: Children: This insulin is approved for children 6 years and older with type 1 diabetes. Use in younger children should be guided by a doctor. Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Blood sugar control is very important during pregnancy, and your insulin dose may need to change. Older Adults: Older adults may be more sensitive to insulin and have a higher risk of low blood sugar. Blood sugar should be monitored carefully. Kidney or Liver Problems: Your dose may need to be adjusted if you have kidney or liver disease, as these conditions can affect how your body uses insulin.
